title: India’s BRICS strategy tested with Xi, Putin set to visit
summary: India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host the 18th BRICS summit this weekend in New Delhi, welcoming Chinese President Xi Jinping to India for the first time since 2019. The summit comes…

blocks.text: India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host the 18th BRICS summit this weekend in New Delhi, welcoming Chinese President Xi Jinping to India for the first time since 2019.

The summit comes at an important moment for India. As New Delhi’s year-long BRICS presidency draws to a close, India is stepping up engagement with China and Russia, and its relationship with Washington remains difficult.

Modi met both Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on August 31 and September 1. Just two weeks later, Modi is set to see them again in New Delhi for the BRICS summit.
But with BRICS both growing in size and increasingly troubled by internal divisions, the forum might limit Modi’s diplomatic gains.
New Delhi and Beijing locked in ‘armed coexistence’ and competition
Indian diplomats are trying to protect their room for maneuver in a changing international order.
Ashok Kantha, a former Indian ambassador to China, said India’s engagement with BRICS and the SCO is part of New Delhi’s longstanding strategy of strategic autonomy.
“These groupings give India a seat at the table and allow it to pursue its own interests while maintaining relationships with different major powers,” Kantha told DW.
However, as Modi prepares to host Xi in New Delhi, ties between India and China are less than ideal.

blocks.caption: India’s geopolitical strategy is heavily impacted by its relationships with both the West and fellow BRICS powersImage: Manish Swarup/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Both countries reached a border patrol agreement in 2024, ending a four-year military standoff along their disputed frontier.

International flights have resumed, the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage has reopened and some visa restrictions have eased. But major problems remain between Beijing and New Delhi — India is reporting a trade deficit of over $112 billion (€96.5 billion) with China, and the two countries argue over market access.
The Modi-Xi meeting will therefore be watched for signs of a major diplomatic thaw, particularly on trade and investment.
Kantha said the visit could bring some stabilization but should not be mistaken for a reset.

“The border remains heavily militarized and major differences over trade, investment and security remain. India needs a stable and predictable relationship with China, but without lowering its guard,” said Kantha.

“It is a relationship of armed coexistence and managed competition. We should not reduce it to a simple ‘elephant and dragon’ story,” he said, referring to traditional symbols of the world’s two most populous nations.
BRICS gets bigger, divisions grow
India’s presidency has already exposed the difficulty of reaching agreement within BRICS, which has grown from its original five members to 11.

blocks.caption: India's BRICS strategy tested with Xi, Putin set to visit

blocks.text: With nations such as Brazil, South Africa, Indonesia and Egypt all part of BRICS, its leaders struggle to reconcile its very different relationships with the US and different interests in conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine. The group now also includes Iran and the UAE, countries that have found themselves on opposing sides of the war in Iran.
Earlier this year, BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement on the Middle East crisis, forcing India to issue a unilateral chair’s statement instead.
With Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian expected at the Delhi summit, this diplomatic divide is likely to take center stage.

“Differences between members such as Iran and the UAE show how difficult it can be to find common ground,” says Harsh Pant, vice president for Studies and Foreign Policy at the Observer Research Foundation.
“BRICS can still work on areas where members share interests, such as reforming global economic governance. But such disagreements are likely to become more common,” he added.
Fears of Chinese dominance
The future of BRICS will also be impacted by the rivalry between India and China.

India wants BRICS to give greater weight to the concerns of developing countries and to support reform of other global institutions such as the United Nations, IMF and World Bank. However, New Delhi does not want the grouping to become a China-led challenge to the West.

India has been pushing for easier cross-border payments between BRICS countries and greater use of national currencies in international trade. At the same time, the Modi government has also been careful not to present this as an attempt to replace the US dollar or create a common BRICS currency.
“Local-currency transactions are likely to become an important area of cooperation,” Pant said, but stressed that India and other BRICS countries are not necessarily seeking ‘de-dollarization.'”
“Instead, they are looking for greater resilience and alternatives to dollar-based financial arrangements.”
India’s ‘America Plus’ strategy

Despite its disagreements with the Trump administration, New Delhi still wants stronger economic and strategic ties with the US, while also maintaining its longstanding relationship with Russia and improving relations with China.
India’s diplomatic course is not a pure “multi-alignment” approach but an “America Plus” strategy, strategic affairs analyst C Raja Mohan told DW.

“India remains dependent on the West for capital, technology, markets and security, while deepening ties with Russia and China for strategic reasons,” said Mohan, a professor of American studies at Jindal Global University.
But this balancing act will become harder as great-power rivalry intensifies, Mohan warns.
“A US-China accommodation could leave India exposed, while Russia’s growing dependence on China is changing the Eurasian balance,” he said.
In this calculation, a more anti-Western BRICS could put pressure on India over its continuing dependence on the West.

The upcoming Delhi summit is likely to show the extent of India’s power — especially as it wraps up its BRICS presidency. For Narendra Modi, the test is whether India can advance its priorities for BRICS and give itself more room to maneuver internationally, without allowing the grouping to become dominated by China or reduced to an anti-Western platform. /dl
